items.title: Format-Aware Fusion for Fast FP4 Pretraining
items.summary: Format-aware fusion is presented to improve fast pretraining using four-bit floating-point (FP4) by co-designing quantization producers with their scale domain and consumer layout. This approach enables native $\text{mxfp}$, global $\text{nvfp}$, and cooperative-thread-array-local $\text{nvfp}$ operations. Evaluation on Llama-3-family 8B pretraining showed that custom routes achieved $37.9\text{K}$ tokens/s/GPU, outperforming bfloat16 and Transformer Engine methods. The results indicated that FP4 outcomes depend on the scale contract, operand, and execution path. This method improved training-loss compared to raw bfloat16, suggesting a benefit beyond raw speed.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "Format-Aware Fusion for Fast FP4 Pretraining" details a method for improving fast pretraining using four-bit floating-point by co-designing quantization producers with their scale domain and consumer layout, achieving notable performance gains. The research introduced format-aware fusion to enable native mxfp, global nvfp, and cooperative-thread-array-local nvfp operations. Evaluation on Llama-3-family 8B pretraining demonstrated that custom routes resulted in thirty-seven point nine thousand tokens per second per GPU, surpassing bfloat16 and Transformer Engine methods. The findings indicated that FP4 outcomes are dependent on the scale contract, operand, and execution path, and this method resulted in improved training loss compared to raw bfloat16. This work suggests a tangible benefit beyond raw speed in the context of large language model pretraining.

items.title: Nous: Learning and Certifying Memory Decisions Before Source Calibration
items.summary: Belief-based agents need reliable decisions despite noisy memory evidence, raising the question of whether memory must calibrate its sources before improving decisions. The work separates learning, calibration, and revision certification within a four-model hidden Markov family. Learning and certifying useful decisions can require quadratically fewer records than source calibration. A certificate can be derived using observable witness regions without needing pure-class anchors. The results statistically account for when memory decisions can be learned and justified without fully recovering source reliability.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "Nous: Learning and Certifying Memory Decisions Before Source Calibration" reports on a framework for belief-based agents that learns and certifies memory decisions before source calibration. The research introduces a method that separates learning, calibration, and revision certification within a four-model hidden Markov family. The work demonstrates that learning and certifying useful decisions can require quadratically fewer records than source calibration. A certificate is shown to be derivable using observable witness regions without requiring pure-class anchors. The results statistically account for instances where memory decisions can be learned and justified without fully recovering source reliability. This work indicates a new approach to building reliable memory systems in artificial intelligence. Future research will focus on applying these certification methods to complex decision-making processes.

items.title: Reverse Item Response Theory for Sparsity-Robust Ranking in Fragmented Cancer Drug-Response Matrices
items.summary: Reverse Item Response Theory is introduced for pharmacogenomic drug-response analysis by modeling cancer types as subjects and drugs as items. The model is applied to 242,036 drug sensitivity measurements from the GDSC2 database to estimate in-vitro resistance and drug activity. Validation shows that reverse IRT better recovers latent rankings than simple averaging across various missingness regimes. The method achieved the best Brier score in held-out prediction, with some cancer types showing stable classifications. Cross-platform replication suggests methodological robustness rather than a universal clinical ranking.
items.audio_script: From arXiv csLG Reverse Item Response Theory for Sparsity-Robust Ranking in Fragmented Cancer Drug-Response Matrices introduces a novel statistical framework for pharmacogenomic drug-response analysis. This research utilizes Reverse Item Response Theory to estimate in-vitro resistance and drug activity by modeling cancer types as subjects and drugs as items. The study applied this model to 242,036 drug sensitivity measurements from the GDSC2 database. The methodology assessed how the model recovers latent rankings when data is incomplete across various missingness regimes. Validation demonstrated that reverse IRT provided superior recovery of latent rankings compared to simple averaging across these missingness scenarios. The method achieved the lowest Brier score in held-out prediction, and certain cancer types exhibited stable classifications in the analysis. Cross-platform replication indicates methodological robustness rather than a universal clinical ranking. Future development should focus on the scalability of this approach in complex biological datasets.

items.title: "very likely" Means "uncertain"? How LLMs Diverge from Humans in Linguistic Uncertainty Quantification
items.summary: Humans express verbal uncertainty through linguistic markers like "very likely," which reflects metacognitive monitoring. Current LLM uncertainty quantification often relies on likelihood or consistency signals rather than these verbal markers. The research investigates how LLMs diverge from humans in verbal uncertainty quantification. A novel algorithm, METHODNAME, is introduced to learn an optimal uncertainty profile directly from marker outputs. This method allows for a direct comparison of confidence semantics between humans and LLMs to reveal systematic confidence disparities.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "very likely" Means "uncertain"? How LLMs Diverge from Humans in Linguistic Uncertainty Quantification. This story investigates the divergence between human and large language model approaches to quantifying linguistic uncertainty. A novel algorithm named METHODNAME was introduced to learn an optimal uncertainty profile directly from linguistic marker outputs, enabling a direct comparison of confidence semantics between humans and LLMs to reveal systematic confidence disparities. Researchers developed this method to analyze how human expression of uncertainty through markers like "very likely" differs from the methods employed by current language models which typically rely on likelihood or consistency signals. The research details the process of applying this algorithm to markers to establish a systematic quantification of confidence. This investigation provides a framework for comparing the semantics of uncertainty expressed by humans against those generated by artificial intelligence systems. The findings suggest a systematic difference in how human and machine systems model and express linguistic uncertainty. This work points toward future developments in aligning AI systems with human modes of probabilistic reasoning.

items.title: How Far is Adam from Natural Gradient Descent?
items.summary: Adam's geometric relationship to Natural Gradient Descent (NGD) is investigated using a scale-invariant metric. The study measures Adam's deviation from NGD across four different loss landscapes, including linear and non-convex settings. Adam's geometric trajectory is found to be context-dependent, showing low deviation in well-conditioned settings but significant misalignment in ill-conditioned neural network problems. While Adam's geometric drift is larger, it does not impair final objective minimization, as Adam consistently achieves low loss. The findings suggest Adam's effectiveness may arise more from structural approximation and momentum smoothing than from closely following the natural gradient path.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "How Far is Adam from Natural Gradient Descent?" investigates the geometric relationship between the Adam optimization algorithm and Natural Gradient Descent. The study found that Adam's geometric trajectory is context-dependent, showing low deviation in well-conditioned settings but significant misalignment in ill-conditioned neural network problems. The researchers employed a scale-invariant metric to measure Adam's deviation from NGD across various loss landscapes, including linear and non-convex settings. The analysis demonstrated that while Adam exhibits a larger geometric drift, it does not compromise the final minimization of the objective function, consistently achieving low loss values. This suggests that Adam's efficacy stems more from structural approximation and momentum smoothing than from precise adherence to the natural gradient path. The findings indicate that the practical performance of adaptive methods is driven by structural properties rather than strict adherence to the natural gradient.

items.title: FourierQK: Filter Shape, Admissibility and the Leakage-Coverage Law
items.summary: Frequency-collapse attention achieves gains by using a bandpass-filtered inner product at a learned frequency. Testing filter properties revealed that DC and Nyquist components are detrimental, confirming the necessity of an oscillatory structure. The optimal single-scale bandwidth is approximately two bins centered around paragraph scale, yielding a performance gain of +1.15 nats. Admissible filters outperform non-admissible Gaussians and provide protection against bilateral FFT leakage. These findings characterize FourierQK for bidirectional attention settings and motivate causal spectral variants for autoregressive models.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "FourierQK: Filter Shape, Admissibility and the Leakage-Coverage Law" details research on frequency-collapse attention and the properties of filtering in attention mechanisms. The study confirmed that using a bandpass-filtered inner product at a learned frequency is beneficial, demonstrating that DC and Nyquist components are detrimental, thereby necessitating an oscillatory structure for optimal performance. The methodology involved testing filter properties to characterize the optimal single-scale bandwidth, which was found to be approximately two bins centered around paragraph scale, resulting in a performance gain of one point one five nats. Furthermore, admissible filters were shown to outperform non-admissible Gaussians and offer protection against bilateral FFT leakage, characterizing FourierQK for bidirectional attention settings. This work motivates the exploration of causal spectral variants for autoregressive models. The findings establish new principles for designing efficient and leakage-resistant spectral representations in attention networks.

items.title: SW-KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Stieltjes-Wigert q-Orthogonal Polynomials
items.summary: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) are proposed as an alternative to traditional deep learning by using learnable univariate functions for node activations. The SW-KAN introduces Stieltjes-Wigert q-orthogonal polynomials to address domain mismatches in polynomial-based KANs. A smooth mapping is used to bridge the domain gap while maintaining stable gradients and efficient evaluation. Experiments show SW-KAN achieves superior accuracy-efficiency in image classification and continuous function approximation tasks. This architecture provides a robust method for efficient function approximation in resource-constrained settings.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "SW-KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Stieltjes-Wigert q-Orthogonal Polynomials" details an advancement in neural network architecture by introducing a method to improve function approximation using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks. The research introduces the SW-KAN, which incorporates Stieltjes-Wigert q-orthogonal polynomials to mitigate domain mismatches encountered in polynomial-based KANs. The methodology involves employing a smooth mapping to bridge the domain gap while preserving stable gradients and efficient evaluation within the network structure. Experimental results demonstrate that the SW-KAN achieves superior accuracy and efficiency in both image classification and continuous function approximation tasks. This architecture presents a robust technique for efficient function approximation, particularly beneficial in resource-constrained computing environments. The findings suggest a pathway toward more effective and efficient function modeling in artificial intelligence systems.

items.title: One Mastery Threshold Does Not Fit All Knowledge Tracing Models
items.summary: A single mastery threshold does not adequately fit all knowledge tracing (KT) models used in tutoring systems. The effectiveness of a threshold varies significantly depending on the underlying KT model, as models like Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) and neural models estimate different aspects of knowledge. Differences in model outputs mean the same numerical cutoff does not represent the same level of mastery across models. Stricter thresholds also failed to reliably reduce performance gaps and could unfairly restrict advancement for stronger-prior students. Therefore, mastery thresholds should be recalibrated based on the specific KT model and instructional priorities.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "One Mastery Threshold Does Not Fit All Knowledge Tracing Models". This report investigates the limitations of using a uniform mastery threshold across various knowledge tracing models in tutoring systems, finding that a single threshold is insufficient for accurately assessing mastery across different models. The study demonstrated that the effectiveness of a mastery threshold is highly dependent on the underlying knowledge tracing model employed, as models such as Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and neural models estimate knowledge in different ways. The research showed that a consistent numerical cutoff does not correspond to the same level of mastery when applied across these different models, and stricter thresholds failed to reliably close performance gaps or restrict advancement equitably for students with stronger prior knowledge. Consequently, the findings suggest that mastery thresholds require recalibration based on the specific knowledge tracing model and instructional objectives. This necessitates a more nuanced approach in designing and implementing AI-driven educational systems.

items.title: Integrating Fairness and Explainability in a Multiple Instance Reinforcement Learning System
items.summary: The study proposes a multi-objective framework combining reinforcement learning-based multiple instance learning (RL-MIL), adversarial debiasing, and preference-conditioned hypernetworks for student-at-risk prediction. The RL agent selects informative instances from student interaction data, treating each student as a bag of weakly labeled interactions. Two hypernetwork variants were tested to see if a user-defined preference scalar could control the trade-off between predictive performance and Equalized Odds. The baseline RL-MIL performs well, but preference conditioning alone fails to guarantee controllable multi-objective behavior due to issues like objective dominance. Robust fair RL-MIL requires explicit mechanisms for gradient balancing and stability analysis.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "Integrating Fairness and Explainability in a Multiple Instance Reinforcement Learning System" details a multi-objective framework combining reinforcement learning-based multiple instance learning, adversarial debiasing, and preference-conditioned hypernetworks for student-at-risk prediction. The research involved an reinforcement learning agent selecting informative instances from student interaction data, treating each student as a bag of weakly labeled interactions. Two hypernetwork variants were assessed to determine if a user-defined preference scalar could regulate the trade-off between predictive performance and Equalized Odds. While the baseline RL-MIL demonstrated performance, preference conditioning alone was insufficient for guaranteed multi-objective control due to objective dominance concerns. Robust fair reinforcement learning multiple instance learning necessitates explicit mechanisms for gradient balancing and stability analysis. This work indicates a need for formalized techniques to ensure fairness and explainability in complex reinforcement learning systems.

items.title: Fast Polynomial Transcendentals for LLMs
items.summary: Short polynomial programs were tested to accelerate special-function unit (SFU) operations in large language models (LLMs). These programs replaced native functions like sigmoid and tanh with degree-3 or degree-4 bfloat16 operations in tasks such as dense SiLU and attention mechanisms. The optimized kernels resulted in performance improvements of 1.19-2.19x in L2 and 1.00-1.70x in HBM memory access. Substitutions in attention improved the attention forward pass by 7.4%. Overall, these optimizations led to noticeable changes in training-loss differences near 100 billion tokens.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.LG, "Fast Polynomial Transcendentals for LLMs" details how short polynomial programs were tested to accelerate special-function unit operations within large language models, resulting in significant performance improvements. The research involved replacing native functions such as sigmoid and tanh with degree-three or degree-four bfloat16 operations in areas like dense SiLU and attention mechanisms. These optimized kernels demonstrated performance gains of one point one nine to two point one nine times in L2 norm and one point zero zero to one point seven zero times in HBM memory access. Furthermore, substitutions within the attention mechanism improved the attention forward pass by seven point four percent, leading to noticeable alterations in training-loss differences observed near one hundred billion tokens. These optimizations indicate a pathway for enhancing the computational efficiency of large language model operations.
